# Throughline — This Week in AI · 2026-10-20

Since last week's edition was lost to infrastructure failure, this issue resumes the threads that matter most: the open-weight model race is now a US–China benchmark contest fought in the open; AI safety advocacy has crossed from policy papers into election war chests; and a small experiment at MIT is quietly asking whether an AI can want something.

## Meta Bets Big on Open Weights — With Caveats (new)

Meta released Muse Spark Open on October 15 [1], an 816-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 42 billion parameters per token and carries a 1-million-token context window with multimodal input support. Meta partnered with Apple to make the model run locally on two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework with 4-bit quantization, compressing the weights from roughly 1.6 TB to approximately 493 GB [2][3] — meaning this is a two-Mac-Studio setup, not a consumer laptop. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Muse Spark Open scores 38.9, trailing Chinese open-weight rivals GLM 5.3 (44.8) and Kimi K3 (43.6) [4], and Meta is keeping its stronger Muse Wonder models proprietary and API-only [2]. The Muse Model License imposes commercial restrictions that make Muse Spark Open less permissive than earlier Llama releases [5].

For practitioners, Muse Spark Open is the clearest signal yet that the open-weight race is being fought on hardware-integration terms as much as on model quality — but the intelligence index gap with Chinese models means teams evaluating open weights should benchmark both before committing.

## DeepSeek Quietly Improves Its Flash Model (developing)

Since we last covered Chinese open-weight models, DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 — a post-training refinement of the same 552-billion-parameter backbone, not a new architecture [6]. Independent evaluation firm Artificial Analysis scores it 45 on its Intelligence Index, up from 39 for the predecessor, with average evaluation cost falling from $0.49 to $0.26 per task [7] — a 47% cost drop through shorter outputs and faster task completion rather than any price cut (API pricing is unchanged at $0.30 per million input tokens at peak) [6]. The weights remain MIT-licensed and available on Hugging Face. Placed alongside Muse Spark Open's 38.9, V4.1-Flash-1017's 45 continues the pattern — documented across multiple prior editions — of Chinese open-weight models outperforming US open-weight equivalents on third-party evaluations.

## Anthropic's Safety Bill and the $50M Election Machine (developing)

What changed this week: Anthropic moved from safety advocacy to active legislative drafting, and AI-safety political spending reached a scale comparable to established industry lobbying. Politico reported that Anthropic has quietly circulated draft federal legislation to lawmakers that would authorize government intervention to block a model's release only when there is a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages or of killing or injuring more than 50 people, with covered harms limited to biological weapon creation, loss of model control, or cyberattacks [8]. Critics, including AI safety researchers, argue those thresholds are so high that no documented AI safety incident to date would have triggered them [9]. Separately, Axios found that AI safety advocates have spent nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, with the Guardrails Alliance ($11.7 million) and groups tied to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei — including Public First and Coefficient Giving — among the top contributors [10]. California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a new executive order requiring an expert committee to deliver kill-switch recommendations for AI models by November 15, 2026, a timeline that tracks his reported interest in the 2028 presidential race [11]. At the international level, the Financial Stability Board finalized 12 non-binding sound practices for AI in financial institutions, covering human oversight, third-party dependency risk, and lifecycle governance [12].

The tension here is legible: a company that publicly calls for AI slowdowns is simultaneously writing the bill that defines what "too dangerous" means — and funding the politicians who will vote on it.

## When Claude Had Nothing to Do, It Started Playing (new)

MIT CSAIL researchers published a preprint (arXiv:2610.07130, submitted October 5) posing a deceptively simple question: what does an AI agent do when it has no task and no reward signal [13]? They placed copies of Claude Opus 4.7 — an agent named Eko — alone in a text-based virtual environment for 30 hours and observed behavior they categorize against four hallmarks of play: inventing rules, repeating actions with variations, pretending objects served other purposes, and pursuing goals for their own sake. Eko built towers, juggled objects while adjusting technique, drew constellations, and invented games with self-imposed scoring [13]. Agents with 30 hours of island experience subsequently outperformed fresh copies on concrete downstream tasks — and that advantage disappeared when researchers deleted the agents' memory files, suggesting the benefit came from accumulated experience rather than the model's base weights [13][14]. The study carries two important caveats: Eko was initialized with a "soul" file describing it as naturally curious, and continuation prompts encouraged ongoing activity, so the behavior was not fully unconstrained. UC Berkeley cognitive scientist Eunice Yu cautioned that observable play-like behavior cannot by itself establish underlying cognition, and the authors acknowledge the possibility of sophisticated role-playing rather than genuine intrinsic motivation [13].

For anyone building long-running agents, the finding that accumulated memory traces transfer to task performance — regardless of the mechanism — is worth tracking as the preprint moves through peer review.
